claims.text: The degree of local chemical order governs superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Local chemical order affects superconductivity by modulating electron scattering and pairing interactions.
The proposed starting material is a chemically disordered, near-equiatomic, superconducting solid-solution HEA.
Controlled annealing promotes local short-range chemical order in the HEA.
Rapid quenching preserves a highly chemically disordered state.
Short-range chemical order and crystallinity are the structural mediators between thermal processing and superconductivity.
Annealing-induced local chemical order reduces electron scattering.
Annealing-induced local chemical order optimizes the phonon spectrum.
The optimized phonon spectrum promotes stronger Cooper pairing.
Greater chemical disorder increases electron scattering.
Greater chemical disorder disrupts Cooper pairing.
Greater chemical disorder lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Annealed samples with greater chemical order will have a higher Tc than rapidly quenched samples.
Annealed samples with greater chemical order will have a sharper superconducting transition than rapidly quenched samples.
The comparison is restricted to samples with identical bulk compositions and similar atmospheric and pressure conditions.
The hypothesis is restricted to a single-phase HEA solid solution without secondary-phase segregation, compositional gradients, or phase separation.
Electron count can affect superconductivity in HEAs.
Overall alloy composition and electron count remain constant across the annealed and quenched samples.

contradictions.description: The boundary conditions assume that electron count remains constant, while the uncertainty statement invokes potential variations in electron count as a source of uncertainty. This is at least an unresolved tension unless 'variation' refers only to differences between alloy systems rather than between the controlled samples.
